meta.title: Who really said "Education is the ability to listen to almost anything without losing your temper or your self-confidence"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Frost really said it — but looser, to Dartmouth’s 1955 graduating class. The tidy aphorism is a condensation credited to him in Reader’s Digest, April 1960.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Education is the ability to listen to almost anything without losing your temper or your self-confidence'?
meta.ogDescription: Robert Frost said a looser version of this to Dartmouth’s 1955 graduates. The famous one-liner is a later condensation — here is the documented source.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Frost really did say this — though not in these words. Addressing Dartmouth’s graduating class in June 1955, he told them they had been “broadened and enlarged to where you can listen to almost anything without losing your temper or your self-confidence.” The tidy one-liner above is a condensation of that sentence, and the source two quotation dictionaries give for it is Reader’s Digest, April 1960 — an issue no accessible archive lets us read, so the exact popular wording cannot be pinned to a primary text.

source.excerpt: You’ve been broadened and enlarged to where you can listen to almost anything without losing your temper or your self-confidence.
trail: June 1955 — Frost speaks at the Dartmouth commencement. His editors record the piece as “Don’t Get Converted. Stay,” an address delivered at the Dartmouth commencement of June 1955 ↗, published in the Dartmouth Alumni Magazine that July.
1972 — Edward Connery Lathem and Lawrance Thompson reprint the address in Robert Frost: Poetry and Prose, where his wording survives intact: “broadened and enlarged to where you can listen…” ↗

1964 — the condensed aphorism is already circulating with a citation attached. James B. Simpson’s Contemporary Quotations prints it as “Robert Frost, Reader’s Digest, April 1960” ↗, and Rhoda Thomas Tripp’s International Thesaurus of Quotations repeats the same citation.
By 1993 — the credit starts falling off. Webster’s 21st Century Book of Quotations runs the line with no author at all ↗.
source.excerptNote: Frost’s own wording, as printed in Robert Frost: Poetry and Prose (1972). It sits inside a passage of advice to the graduating class about accepting an opponent’s premises instead of contradicting them; only the sentence itself is reproduced here, as the text remains in copyright.

source.rightsNote: The text quoted here is the one printed in Robert Frost: Poetry and Prose, which carries a 1972 copyright by Holt, Rinehart and Winston, Inc., and Frost’s prose is still under active rights management by his estate. The 1955 date alone would not settle it: United States works published between 1929 and 1963 entered the public domain unless their copyright was renewed in the twenty-eighth year, so the 1972 collection, not the age of the address, is what the in-copyright status rests on. The single sentence is quoted here for identification and verification.

author.name: Robert Frost
author.heading: Robert Frost
author.metaLine: 1874–1963 · American poet · spoke at Dartmouth’s June 1955 commencement
author.bio: Frost built a career out of plain New England speech that turns out, on second reading, to be argument. He had a long and tangled relationship with Dartmouth: he enrolled as a young man and left within months, then came back across his life as a speaker and honorary graduate — the first person to receive two honorary degrees from the college (1933 and 1955). The 1955 commencement address that produced this line is Frost in his late public register: conversational, a little sly, and giving practical advice about how to disagree.

misattribution.heading: Not a misattribution — a compression
misattribution.intro: Nobody stole this line from Frost, and no rival claimant has a better case. What happened is smaller and more ordinary: a loose spoken sentence was tightened into an aphorism, and then the anthologies went to work on the aphorism.

items.why: Frost’s documented sentence is second-person and much looser — “You’ve been broadened and enlarged to where you can listen to almost anything…” ↗. The familiar “Education is the ability to…” opening does not appear anywhere in Robert Frost: Poetry and Prose, the standard one-volume edition of his prose, nor in Lathem’s Interviews with Robert Frost.
A run of speakers’ handbooks and classroom books prints only the first half — “without losing your temper. —Robert Frost” ↗ — dropping the self-confidence clause that does most of the work.
Webster’s 21st Century Book of Quotations runs the line with no author at all, just “—Anonymous” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Frost’s and he said it out loud to a graduating class; the sentence you see quoted is a tidied-up version of it, and the source the quotation dictionaries point to for that version is Reader’s Digest, April 1960 ↗.

context.heading: Why the tidy version travels and the real one doesn’t
lead: Frost’s sentence is second-person and conversational: he is telling a specific room of graduating students what four years has done to them. The version that spread is third-person and definitional — education is the ability to… — and definitions are what anthologies, speakers’ handbooks and teacher gift books are shopping for. The compression is not a distortion of his meaning so much as a change of grammatical mood, and that change is exactly what made the line portable.

There is a small irony in it. A sentence about listening to almost anything without losing your self-confidence lost its own footing twice over: first its author’s phrasing, then — in at least one widely sold reference book — his name.
context.detailsSummary: What Frost was actually telling the graduates
detailsBody: The passage is advice about how to argue. Frost’s formula, in his words, is to politely accept the other person’s premises rather than contradict them — take the argument up where it is handed to you, and then show what you can make of it. The line about listening without losing your temper is the pay-off of that advice, not a definition of education.

He then reaches for an example: a student out of the ‘Bible belt’ who is confronted with the fact of evolution and is supposed to be shaken about God by it. Read in place, the sentence is a claim about surviving disagreement — narrower, and better, than the poster version.

sourcesVerified.claim: Robert Frost: Poetry and Prose (1972) contains the sentence "You've been broadened and enlarged to where you can listen to almost anything without losing your temper or your self-confidence", which also appears in The Dartmouth Reader and The Robert Frost Reader.
Lathem and Thompson's acknowledgement in Robert Frost: Poetry and Prose describes "Don't Get Converted. Stay" as an address delivered at the Dartmouth commencement of June 1955.
James B. Simpson's Contemporary Quotations and Rhoda Thomas Tripp's International Thesaurus of Quotations both attribute the condensed aphorism to "Robert Frost, Reader's Digest, April 1960".
A run of speakers' handbooks and classroom books prints the line truncated at "without losing your temper", still credited to Robert Frost.
Webster's 21st Century Book of Quotations prints the line credited to "Anonymous".
The Internet Archive holds a lending copy of Robert Frost: Poetry and Prose (1972).
Dartmouth's complete magazine archive holds the July 1955 issue of the Dartmouth Alumni Magazine.
Wikiquote's Robert Frost page does not list this quotation in any section, and the word "temper" does not appear on the page.
Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation; a search for "without losing your temper" returns nothing found.
Robert Frost's dates are March 26, 1874 - January 29, 1963.

Dartmouth has conferred honorary doctorates twice upon two of its alumni: Robert Frost (in 1933 and 1955) and Nelson Rockefeller (in 1957 and 1969) - so Frost was the first, not the only, person to hold two.

The Dartmouth Alumni Magazine of July 1955 prints the full text of Frost's June 1955 commencement address, including "You've been broadened and enlarged to where you can listen to almost anything without losing your temper or your self-confidence".
